stem: A $2.0\text{ kg}$ trolley moving at $3.0\text{ m s}^{-1}$ collides with a stationary $1.0\text{ kg}$ trolley and they move off together. What is the speed of the trolleys after the collision?
markscheme: Momentum is conserved: $2.0 \times 3.0 = 3.0\,v$, so $v = 2.0\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

help.title: Which law applies?
help.text: Two trolleys collide and no external force acts on them. What quantity is conserved in every collision like this?

help.title: Momentum before
help.text: **Momentum** is conserved. Before: $p = 2.0 \times 3.0 + 1.0 \times 0 = 6.0\text{ kg m s}^{-1}$.

help.title: Momentum after
help.text: They move off together, so treat them as one object of mass $3.0\text{ kg}$ with speed $v$: $p = 3.0\,v$.

help.title: Final answer
help.text: $3.0\,v = 6.0$, so $v = 2.0\text{ m s}^{-1}$. The answer is **C**.

stem: A resultant force of $12\text{ N}$ acts on a $4.0\text{ kg}$ object for $2.0\text{ s}$. What is the change in momentum of the object?
markscheme: Impulse $= F\Delta t = 12 \times 2.0 = 24\text{ N s}$ = change in momentum. The mass is not needed.

help.title: Which idea links force and time?
help.text: A force acting for a time gives an **impulse**. How is impulse related to change in momentum?

help.title: Impulse = change in momentum
help.text: $\Delta p = F\Delta t$. Do you need the mass to use this?

help.title: Final answer
help.text: No, the mass is not needed. $\Delta p = 12 \times 2.0 = 24\text{ N s}$, so the answer is **C**.

stem: A car of mass $1200\text{ kg}$ travelling at $15\text{ m s}^{-1}$ brakes uniformly and comes to rest in $3.0\text{ s}$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the magnitude of the deceleration of the car.

help.title: Definition
help.text: Acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the time taken: $a = \dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$.

help.title: Change in velocity
help.text: The car goes from $15\text{ m s}^{-1}$ to rest, so the size of the change is $15\text{ m s}^{-1}$, over $3.0\text{ s}$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the average braking force on the car.

help.title: Which law?
help.text: Newton's second law connects force, mass and acceleration: $F = ma$.

help.title: Substitute
help.text: Use $m = 1200\text{ kg}$ and your deceleration from (a).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State Newton's third law of motion. Identify the force that pairs with the frictional force of the road on the car.
markscheme: If body A exerts a force on body B, then B exerts a force of equal magnitude and opposite direction on A (forces of the same type)
The frictional force of the car (tyres) on the road, acting forwards

help.title: Recall the law
help.text: Newton's third law is about pairs of forces between **two** bodies. What do you know about their sizes, directions and types?

help.title: Statement
help.text: If body A exerts a force on body B, then B exerts a force on A that is **equal in size, opposite in direction and of the same type**.

help.title: Swap the bodies
help.text: The force in the question is friction **of the road on the car**. Its partner is the same type of force with the two bodies swapped.

help.title: Final answer
help.text: The pair is the frictional force **of the car (its tyres) on the road**, acting forwards.

parts.label: d
parts.text: A seat belt stretches slightly during a sudden stop. Outline why this reduces the force on a passenger.
markscheme: The change in momentum of the passenger is the same
but it takes place over a longer time, so $F = \Delta p / \Delta t$ is smaller

help.title: What doesn't change?
help.text: Whatever the seat belt does, the passenger goes from moving to stopped. So their change in momentum $\Delta p$ is fixed.

help.title: The key equation
help.text: Force is the rate of change of momentum: $F = \dfrac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}$. What does stretching do to $\Delta t$?

help.title: Final answer
help.text: The change in momentum is the same, but stretching makes it happen over a **longer time**, so $F = \Delta p / \Delta t$ is **smaller**.

stem:
A student pulls a trolley along a horizontal bench with different constant forces $F$ and measures the acceleration $a$ each time.

F / N: 0.50, 1.00, 1.50, 2.00
a / m s⁻²: 0.24, 0.51, 0.74, 1.01

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the data to determine the mass of the trolley.
markscheme: Mass is the gradient of a graph of $F$ against $a$ (or uses $\Delta F / \Delta a$ from two well-separated points)

help.title: Link the graph to F = ma
help.text: $F = ma$. If you plot $F$ on the y-axis against $a$ on the x-axis, you get a straight line. What does its gradient represent?

help.title: Gradient = mass
help.text: The gradient is $\dfrac{\Delta F}{\Delta a} = m$. Use two points far apart, such as the first and last readings.

help.title: Final answer
help.text: $m \approx 1.9$ to $2.0\text{ kg}$

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why a graph of $F$ against $a$ might not pass exactly through the origin.
markscheme: Friction acts on the trolley, so some of the applied force is needed before it accelerates (or any reasonable systematic error, e.g. a zero error in the force meter)

help.title: Think about the intercept
help.text: If the line misses the origin, some force is applied but produces no acceleration. Which force on the trolley could be cancelling part of the pull?

help.title: Final answer
help.text: **Friction** on the trolley: part of the applied force is needed to overcome it. (A zero error in the force meter is also accepted.)
